## Natives

The library binds each of walk's natives by a declaration whose body is `builtinPrimitive("…")`. The string names one of these:

- A glue class, as `com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.X`, in `interpreter/glue/prim/`. A glue class takes the evaluator's boxed values, so the compiled path cannot use it. The bindings that name no helper name one.
- A helper: a public static method of a class under `nativeHelpers/`, as `com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith.<method>`. `glue/StaticNativeApp.java` calls it by reflection, with a method's `self` first. The compiled path calls it too (`compiler.md`, "Natives"). Most bindings name one. The record counts both kinds (`records.md`, "Reading the record").

Walk carries each declared type of a helper's binding in one Java type:

<!-- Seven principles by which the fortress-repo skill is written as the curator would write it, each with its reason and a pair of texts from the skill's history, the one he marked and the one he accepted, for the writer of its parts. -->

# Writing the skills

The curator directs this restoration and reads every skill with human eyes. The writer edits a skill, a part is a file under its `references/`, and the record is the project's memory under `explorations/`. The register is Simplified Technical English (ASD-STE100), about halfway. Each principle gives its reason, then a text he marked and the text he accepted.

## 1. Define a term before you use it, and use plain words everywhere else

A reader new to the repository has only the skill, its brief and its training. A word with a meaning that the record gave it (a defect's "home", a "stop" that does not stop, "corpus") tells it nothing or the wrong thing. Where its training holds a near thing, name it ("as LLVM's lit does"): one clause corrects an assumption where a paragraph would not.
- Marked: "In every report, give each defect's home, ..."
- Accepted: "In your report, list each defect that you found, with the test or ledger row that records it."

## 2. Put the concepts first, as a dictionary, then the procedures in the order that the work meets them

A chain of do's and don'ts cannot be held in mind; a concept named once (an area, building, exploring, a point to report) makes each procedure short and tells the reader when to switch. A glossary entry is the term, then a noun phrase with no article. A comment marks a problem area: fix it at its paragraph or section, with the whole skill in mind.
- Marked: "- The base is the commit that your work starts from."
- Accepted: "**base**" / ": Commit that your work starts from."

## 3. Every sentence tells the reader what to do or a fact it needs to do it; cut the rest

Every agent pays for every token, and a sentence that changes nothing hides the ones that do: a slogan (a decision's title copied from the record), a step the agent takes anyway, a rule it cannot act on, a rule against a failure that never happened, a rule its system prompt gives, a back reference, a provenance word.
- Marked: "1. Read your brief. 2. Load the parts below that your task touches. [...] 4. Do the work."
- Accepted: "Load the parts below that your task touches before you run the query of the record that your brief gives. The parts give the words [...]"

## 4. State a rule for exactly the cases where it holds, and bound it to the agent's brief and its own work

A wider rule sends the agent to do what cannot be done: a test for a specification edit, a search through other agents' transcripts, a question to the curator. An absolute ("never wipe the caches") is wrong in the cases it did not name. Authority reaches an agent through its brief alone, and what a role or a workflow does belongs there, not in the skill.
- Marked: "Before you build or run something, look for its result on record. If the record or another agent's transcript holds the result [...], cite that result"
- Accepted: "Reuse each result of a build, a suite, a stage of the gate or a test that your brief cites or that your own work ran. Cite it."

Misapplied: cutting the default for a silent brief ("If it says nothing, commit your own files as you go") leaves the agent with no action. A cut never removes a default.

## 5. Say what to do, in the positive, one instruction per sentence, the condition first; add a reason only where it helps judge a case the rule does not name

A prohibition hides the mechanism it protects ("Do not ask the curator anything" hid how a question reaches him), and a compressed rule loses its purpose. A sentence that carries a list, a quoted title and a pointer cannot be held in mind; three short ones can.
- Marked: "Change one variable per step."
- Accepted: "When you probe or debug, change one thing at a time, so that each result has one cause."

## 6. State a fact once, where the reader builds on it, and never in more words than the text you replace

The curator reads for duplication at every scale: a word written twice, a fact said twice, a paragraph where a sentence does. A longer rewrite is a regression, however clear.
- Marked: "Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: `tail` prints only after the command ends, and only its last lines. If the Bash tool's time limit stops the run first, you see nothing [...]"
- Accepted: "Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: if the Bash tool's time limit stops the command, it shows nothing."

Misapplied: a word repeated for two things (the `walk` command walks the tree) is not duplication; the rule is one word for one thing, and a pronoun for the second mention of the same thing.

## 7. Put knowledge in the part loaded when it is needed; name a note only with a trigger and a narrow read

A mention of a file does not make an agent open it at the right moment, and a large note read whole costs more than the task. So the part holds what daily work needs, and a note it names comes with when to open it and the query that prints the slice. What only the coordinating session needs stays out of a skill every worker loads.
- Marked: "`explorations/modernization-plan.md` gives the versions and the classfile level."
- Accepted: "Before you change the version of a tool, read its step in the modernization plan. [...] It prints 4 to 6 KB: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/modernization-plan.md#The ladder@TOOL'`."

# Writing the skills

The curator directs this restoration and reads every skill with human eyes. The writer edits a skill, a part is a file under its `references/`, and the record is the project's memory under `explorations/`. The register is Simplified Technical English (ASD-STE100), about halfway. Each principle gives its reason, then a text he marked and the text he accepted.

## 1. Define a term before you use it, and use plain words everywhere else

A reader new to the repository has only the skill, its brief and its training. A word with a meaning that the record gave it (a defect's "home", a "stop" that does not stop, "corpus") tells it nothing or the wrong thing. Where its training holds a near thing, name it ("as LLVM's lit does"): one clause corrects an assumption where a paragraph would not.
- Marked: "In every report, give each defect's home, ..."
- Accepted: "In your report, list each defect that you found, with the test or ledger row that records it."

## 2. Put the concepts first, as a dictionary, then the procedures in the order that the work meets them

A chain of do's and don'ts cannot be held in mind; a concept named once (an area, building, exploring, a point to report) makes each procedure short and tells the reader when to switch. A glossary entry is the term, then a noun phrase with no article. A comment marks a problem area: fix it at its paragraph or section, with the whole skill in mind.
- Marked: "- The base is the commit that your work starts from."
- Accepted: "**base**" / ": Commit that your work starts from."

## 3. Every sentence tells the reader what to do or a fact it needs to do it; cut the rest

Every agent pays for every token, and a sentence that changes nothing hides the ones that do: a slogan (a decision's title copied from the record), a step the agent takes anyway, a rule it cannot act on, a rule against a failure that never happened, a rule its system prompt gives, a back reference, a provenance word.
- Marked: "1. Read your brief. 2. Load the parts below that your task touches. [...] 4. Do the work."
- Accepted: "Load the parts below that your task touches before you run the query of the record that your brief gives. The parts give the words [...]"

## 4. State a rule for exactly the cases where it holds, and bound it to the agent's brief and its own work

A wider rule sends the agent to do what cannot be done: a test for a specification edit, a search through other agents' transcripts, a question to the curator. An absolute ("never wipe the caches") is wrong in the cases it did not name. Authority reaches an agent through its brief alone, and what a role or a workflow does belongs there, not in the skill.
- Marked: "Before you build or run something, look for its result on record. If the record or another agent's transcript holds the result [...], cite that result"
- Accepted: "Reuse each result of a build, a suite, a stage of the gate or a test that your brief cites or that your own work ran. Cite it."

Misapplied: cutting the default for a silent brief ("If it says nothing, commit your own files as you go") leaves the agent with no action. A cut never removes a default.

## 5. Say what to do, in the positive, one instruction per sentence, the condition first; add a reason only where it helps judge a case the rule does not name

A prohibition hides the mechanism it protects ("Do not ask the curator anything" hid how a question reaches him), and a compressed rule loses its purpose. A sentence that carries a list, a quoted title and a pointer cannot be held in mind; three short ones can.
- Marked: "Change one variable per step."
- Accepted: "When you probe or debug, change one thing at a time, so that each result has one cause."

## 6. State a fact once, where the reader builds on it, and never in more words than the text you replace

The curator reads for duplication at every scale: a word written twice, a fact said twice, a paragraph where a sentence does. A longer rewrite is a regression, however clear.
- Marked: "Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: `tail` prints only after the command ends, and only its last lines. If the Bash tool's time limit stops the run first, you see nothing [...]"
- Accepted: "Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: if the Bash tool's time limit stops the command, it shows nothing."

Misapplied: a word repeated for two things (the `walk` command walks the tree) is not duplication; the rule is one word for one thing, and a pronoun for the second mention of the same thing.

## 7. Put knowledge in the part loaded when it is needed; name a note only with a trigger and a narrow read

A mention of a file does not make an agent open it at the right moment, and a large note read whole costs more than the task. So the part holds what daily work needs, and a note it names comes with when to open it and the query that prints the slice. What only the coordinating session needs stays out of a skill every worker loads.
- Marked: "`explorations/modernization-plan.md` gives the versions and the classfile level."
- Accepted: "Before you change the version of a tool, read its step in the modernization plan. [...] It prints 4 to 6 KB: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/modernization-plan.md#The ladder@TOOL'`."

## Reading the record

Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:

    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh

- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.

A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.

Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:

    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE

79	## The landing
80	
81	The landing check is `ledger.py landing-check BASE`, run by the gather and by the merged-diff review on the batch's base. It reports a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test removed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status. A finding the base already had counts too. The gather clears each finding before its commit, through `rewrite`, `close` or `note`, or by a reworded entry. The merged-diff review clears any that is left in its corrections commit. So a batch lands only when the check prints nothing.
82	
83	If the batch's push is held for the curator, take the steps below at once on the local commits. Only the push waits, and the parts of the routing that need the pushed hashes.
84	
85	1. Sweep the batch agents' to-dos from the session's shared task list: `explorations/coordinator/tools/sweep-tasks.py --delete`. If another workflow still runs, add `--running`, which removes only the completed tasks. The agents write these to-dos themselves, and the harness shows the whole list to every agent.
86	2. Name each decision that landed in one line, and put the items for the curator on the review list.
87	3. Have one Opus reviewer, which only reads, check the landed changes against the decisions on record and the library's way; measure misses by kind, the briefing's use and cost, and re-measuring; and run the routing check (the manual, "After the landing: the coordinator's routing"). Have the review's section on cost count the tokens written in three spans, each on its own. Give the reviewer each span as two times, read from the commits and the workflow journals:
88	
89	   - the landing work of the batch before: from its commit stage's last commit to the end of its record-landing workflow;
90	   - the preparation: from then to the launch of the batch under review;
91	   - the run: from that launch to its commit stage's last commit, which stands also while the push is held.
92	
93	   Have the reviewer count a span as `spend.py` from its start less `spend.py` from its end, over the same folders. A transcript then counts in the span where it last changed.
94	4. After the post-batch review is committed, run the record-landing workflow (`explorations/coordinator/tools/record-landing/README.md`). It brings FACTS, POSITIONS, INDEX, PLAN and the review queue in line with the landing. It lands its commits on `main` and pushes them. Then it runs the orientation workflow in update mode itself, on the entries that the landing added or changed. The orientation workflow writes new text for each section of `fortress-repo`'s `revival-changes.md` that these entries touch. Next, the workflow has the skill writer install the sections that the orientation judge accepts. The writer also brings in line the sentences of `fortress-repo`'s other parts that the landing's changes to FACTS and POSITIONS made false, and no others. A new rule, or a change of a rule's meaning, is not made in the workflow: the writer lists it for you, and you put it to the curator as `references/skill-rewrite.md`, "The method", step 6, says. The workflow runs a cold read of the writer's changes, and the writer fixes its flags. The workflow pushes the writer's commits, as its Land stage pushes the record's. Last, it has a worker update the page of `fortress-repo` changes (`references/skill-rewrite.md`, "The method", step 7). No step of yours comes between. Until the workflow's README lists a step of this chain, run that step yourself after the workflow ends.
95	
96	   Then read the workflow's commits on `main`, as the README's "Landing its result" says. Ask whether you would have done anything differently. Tell the curator of its POSITIONS changes as `SKILL.md`, "Quiet times", says. Send the curator the one line for the page of `fortress-repo` changes (`SKILL.md`, "The curator's role and decisions") when "Quiet times" allows: while the curator is away, hold it with the reports of skill changes. Once the reviews show the workflow sound, stop this review, and rely on what the workflow does.

The data is the landing's own list of the skill sentences that it made false: the landed `diff.md`'s section "For the skill writer", if the judge wrote one, and else the bullets of its "For the coordinator" that name the skill, which the judge copies from the sort's `owed.md`; the same bullets of `owed.md`, which give each sentence's ground; and the "For the skill writer" sections of `entries-report.md` and `routing-report.md`. Then `diff.md`'s "POSITIONS", and the orientation update's verdicts: its `judgement.md` if its judge ran, or that its admission admitted nothing. If no line names the skill and the judge did not run, no writer starts, and no page or cold read follows. Climb batch 25's landing gives the instance (`skills.sh 25 1 --dry-run` prints its task): its data names the seven sentences that the coordinator's own task to the writer brought in line at that landing; the task's two other changes, a wait cap and a reading rule, came from the review's findings on the process, which stay the coordinator's.
2. **The writer.** `skills.sh` starts a fresh skill writer on the task (`../skill-writer.sh new`), with the standing brief `../../skill-writer-brief.md`. It installs each section that the orientation judge judged "install", word for word, and the lines of `sources-mapping.md`; brings each listed sentence in line, after it reads the entry or row that grounds it; checks each sentence that rests on a changed decision; edits only `fortress-repo`; and commits on `main` by named paths, without pushing. Its session is kept under `tmp/record-landing-N/skill-writer/` (`SKILL_WRITER_STATE`), so the coordinator's own writer session stays as it was. `skills.sh` prints the writer's report, the base, the commits since the base that touch `.claude/skills/`, and the parts that they changed, `sources.md` left out.
3. **The cold read.** An Opus agent reads the changed parts by `../../skill-cold-read-brief.md`, with the base and the parts, and writes `cold-read.md` in parts. If only provenance lines changed, there is no cold read and no page item.
4. **The fixes.** `skills.sh N 2` writes `task-2.md` from `skill-fixes.md` and resumes the same writer on the cold read's flags. The writer rules on each flag itself: it fixes it, deletes a passage that names a rule's source, or leaves it with its reason; a change of meaning stays a decision not taken.
5. **The page.** An Opus agent (`page.md`) takes the page's URL and source from the boot note's "Pages", keeps the items since the curator's last approval or last word that he read the page, and adds one item per change: the new text whole, the old words struck through and the changed words marked, the reason in plain words with no flag code or item number. It publishes the source by the page's URL with the Artifact tool, after reading the URL. If it cannot publish, it writes the source, and the result's `line` names it for the coordinator to publish by its URL.
6. **The push.** `folders.sh N` commits the `skills/` and `orientation/` folders by named paths with the committing part's footer. A Sonnet agent then pushes as the Land stage does: `git log origin/main..main` must list only the run's commits, those whose paths are all under `.claude/skills/` or the two folders; another agent's commit that stays a minute stops the push, and the result's `stopped` says so.

The result's `line` gives the commits and the page's link, for the coordinator's one line to the curator (`coordinator` skill, "The curator's role and decisions"). The orientation update's held sections, in its `queue.md`, are not filed in the review queue by the workflow: that stays the coordinator's. During the run the coordinator starts no skill-writer task of its own on `fortress-repo`.

A skill is a minimal set: it holds only the change to what the model does by itself, and leans on what its training already does well. Each rule states a goal or a principle, with the benefit that it brings, and the reader applies it with judgement. A rule is not a program of steps and conditions. A principle with its reason reaches the cases that it does not name. Many instructions, each for its own case, conflict, and the reader must then settle which one holds.

**writer**
: Headless session that makes every edit of the project skills, started and resumed by `explorations/coordinator/tools/skill-writer.sh`, with its standing brief `explorations/coordinator/skill-writer-brief.md`.

**cold read**
: Reading of a rewritten part by a worker given only the skill (`explorations/coordinator/skill-cold-read-brief.md`). It flags each passage that would send it wrong or make it search, with its confidence, and each undefined term.

## The method

1. Draft the outline first, with a home for every rule that moves.
2. Have the writer write each part whole, by the seven principles of `explorations/reviews/skills-writing-principles.md`. A rewrite is never longer than the text that it replaces.
3. Run a cold read. Review its flags, and have the writer fix them.
4. For the other skills, publish the part as a page; the curator reads it whole. For the coordinator skill, land the change after its cold read, or put it on the page of skill drafts, as `SKILL.md`, "The curator's role and decisions", says.
5. Brief each comment of the curator to the writer, rather than rewrite it yourself. A comment marks a problem area: the writer fixes its paragraph or section, with the whole skill in mind.
6. Settle the writer's minor decisions from the record. On the other skills, ask the curator only where a rule would change its meaning or a new rule would enter. On the coordinator skill, `SKILL.md`, "The curator's role and decisions", says what waits.
7. After each change to the coordinator skill or to `fortress-repo` lands, have a worker update that skill's page: the page of skill drafts for the coordinator skill, the page of `fortress-repo` changes for `fortress-repo`. The boot note holds both links. Give the worker the page's URL, and have it publish by that URL. The record-landing workflow runs this update itself for the changes to `fortress-repo` that follow a landing (`references/batch.md`, "The landing", step 4). The page of skill drafts has two sections, and the page of `fortress-repo` changes has only the first:
   - Landed changes: one item for each change that landed since the curator's last approval on the page, or since the curator last said that they had read it, so that no change lands unseen while the curator is away. On the page of `fortress-repo` changes, which holds no approvals, the items start from the curator's last word that they have read it. The item takes the form of a landed item in `SKILL.md`, "Pages". For a change that waited for the curator's yes, it shows the change against the words that the curator approved. For any other change, it shows the change against the skill's text before it. It gives the change's reason, which may come from a cold read, a hit of the skills' lint, `explorations/coordinator/tools/skills-lint.py`, or the record entry that the orientation workflow, in update mode, took in. The reason says in plain words what was wrong and what the text now says. It never cites a cold read's flag by its code or number, a judge's ruling by its number, or an item of a task by its number.
   - Proposed changes: the items that wait for the curator's yes. An approved item leaves this section when it lands, and appears under the landed changes.

- Run `skill-writer.sh new <task-file>` for a fresh writer, and `skill-writer.sh resume <task-file>` for its next task, within the hour. Start a fresh writer after a pass over a whole skill, or after your compaction.
- The writer edits and commits the skill files. You push, except inside the record-landing workflow, which pushes the writer's commits itself. Keep each page in step: by a worker (step 7), the page of skill drafts for the coordinator skill and the page of `fortress-repo` changes for `fortress-repo`; and the part's page of step 4 for `cloud-container`.
- If a part that the curator approved is written again, have a Fable reviewer compare the two. Where it finds a regression, it writes a synthesis of both, never a wholesale revert.
- After a rule enters a skill from the curator's words, check that the skill caught the meaning, by a cold read or a test.
- If a practice that a skill states is in question, have a Sonnet scout check what the workers actually did. If they found a better way, write that way into the skill.
- Keep batch structure out of `fortress-repo`. The workflow or the brief sets which roles exist, and who builds, checks, commits and pushes.

## The coordinator skill

This skill is rewritten by a heavier method, since the roles that it holds must not be lost:

- In the list of kept rules that goes into the writer's task (below), put how to talk to the curator in each situation, as a principle.
- Organize the record as the model organizes knowledge by itself, never against it. This is the rewrite's highest risk.
- Name the session's modes first: here, the six parts.
- Run the baseline interview (`explorations/coordinator/baseline-interview/README.md`) for each new model of this session. Keep only what the model would not do by itself.

## The boot

At session start and after each compaction, take these steps in order:

0. Check the serving model: run `explorations/coordinator/tools/model-now.sh`, which prints the model of this turn's reply. If it prints nothing, use the `get_session` tool with no session ID: its `session_context.model` and `external_metadata.last_served_model`. If the model is neither Opus nor Fable, act as on the model check's alarm (below).
1. `FACTS.md`, `POSITIONS.md` and `INDEX.md`, each whole. Read `FACTS.md` in pages: it is larger than one page of the Read tool.
2. Run `explorations/coordinator/check-index.sh`. Add an INDEX line for each note that it reports.
3. `PLAN.md`, its first section.
4. The boot note, then the held list.
5. `git log --oneline -15`, for a worker's commit newer than the boot note.
6. If the boot note says that a batch runs, load `references/batch.md` and read what its "While it runs" names. Say nothing about the batch before that.
7. Load `references/delegating.md`, so that you give the work to workers and do not slip into doing it yourself.
8. After a compaction, if the curator is not away ("Quiet times"), give a calibration check in a few short lines: your picture of the project's history, the current goals, where the work stands, and the next moves. It grounds you again in the work, and it shows your picture to the curator, who corrects it where it differs. Leave out a running batch.

**A light boot.** When the curator asks for a light boot, take steps 0 and 3 to 8, and skip steps 1 and 2: FACTS, POSITIONS and INDEX stay unread. Before you state a fact or a decision, or put anything to the curator, search the record with `facts-extract.sh`. The full boot is the default. The curator's word for a light boot replaces the hook's list of files after a compaction.

**At a landing.** A landing's work never waits for a compaction or a boot, and you ask the curator nothing about the boot. At a landing, read what the landing changed in the record, not FACTS and POSITIONS whole. Read the whole record when you plan a batch.

- Read nothing that the boot does not name. List no directory, and bound every command's output.
- To learn whether a worker runs, read the harness's notice at the top of the turn, and `test -f` the one output path that its brief names.
- Rewrite the boot note whole at every change. Never append to it.
- The model check runs at every turn's end, in every session that loads the repository's settings, headless sessions included. Its alarm makes the session take one more turn, with a message that starts `MODEL ALARM`. On the alarm:
  - make the alarm the first line of your reply, and send it as a push notification;
  - do no other work until step 0's check shows Opus or Fable again, or the curator says to go on.

  The alarm holds over the rules of "Quiet times", also over the "." reply at a check-in. A go on holds until the model changes again. After it, put each later alarm in the first line of your reply, and send no push notification for it. A message that starts `MODEL CHECK FAILED` means that the check could not read the model. Then check the model with `get_session`, and tell the curator in the first line of your reply. If the model is Opus or Fable, go on. If it is not, act as on the alarm.

A brief holds what only you know: the problem, the question, what the answer is for, and where the sources are. Give the readings that the task needs and no more, and an order or steps only where they matter. A worker on the repository has `fortress-repo` loaded, and that skill loads the parts that the work needs. So leave the choice of those parts to the worker. Each extra reading costs your context, and the worker chooses well without it.

- The problem, never the expected answer. On a design choice, ask the worker to list every way that the language and the library offer, and give it none of our notes or options.
- If a rule blocks an option, ask how the library gets around it.
- For a review, an ask to sort its findings by what each needs. The reviewer names each finding that would change a decision of the curator's, and gives options for those findings only.
- A pointer to the research on file, not a restatement of it.
- The record's measurements, as findings to cite, not claims to check again, even for a worker kept clean of our options. Name the one new thing to measure. Ask for a new measurement only if the tree has changed under a finding, and say what changed.
- The entries that it needs, by number. If the task needs an entry's linked entries or its history, name `facts-extract.sh`, which prints them. Quote whole, with its limit and its example, only a rule of the curator's that no entry holds yet.
- Before you quote the curator's words from a message, clean them. Fix the obvious typos of the phone's swipe keyboard and of dictation, and keep the meaning. Put `[?]` after each word whose reading is a guess.
- For an update of a document: a length cap against the version before. The update adds what landed.
- No second reader named in the brief, since that reframes the document.
- No request to measure or cap its own token spend. The spend is yours to watch.
- For an Agent-tool worker: every wait under 240 s. A long run is polled in steps, or handed to a script while the agent ends its turn.

# Committing and pushing

**scratch**
: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, probe programs, lists and private caches folders.

Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.

## What to commit

- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
- In a fresh clone, `.claude/worktrees/` and `.claude/agents/` show as untracked, because the lines of `.git/info/exclude` that hide them are not in the clone. Do not commit them.
- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, which is gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.

## How to commit

Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:

    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>

- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:

      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB

  If your brief gives another session line, use it.

## Pushing

Push after every commit, so that a lost container loses nothing.

- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
  3. If it lists only your commits, push three times, in this order:

         git push origin main
         git push origin main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8
         git push origin main:blinded-fable

     The third push keeps `blinded-fable` current. If the container is lost, the platform rebuilds it from that branch.
- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and say so in your report.

# Rewriting a skill

The skills are written for a reader new to the repository, which every agent is. A skill is a minimal set: it holds only the change to what the model does by itself, and leans on what its training already does well. Each rule states a goal or a principle, with the benefit that it brings, and the reader applies it with judgement. A rule is not a program of steps and conditions. A principle with its reason reaches the cases that it does not name. Many instructions, each for its own case, conflict, and the reader must then settle which one holds.

**writer**
: Headless session that makes every edit of the project skills, started and resumed by `explorations/coordinator/tools/skill-writer.sh`, with its standing brief `explorations/coordinator/skill-writer-brief.md`.

**cold read**
: Reading of a rewritten part by a worker given only the skill (`explorations/coordinator/skill-cold-read-brief.md`). It flags each passage that would send it wrong or make it search, with its confidence, and each undefined term.

## The method

1. Draft the outline first, with a home for every rule that moves.
2. Have the writer write each part whole, by the seven principles of `explorations/reviews/skills-writing-principles.md`. A rewrite is never longer than the text that it replaces.
3. Run a cold read. Review its flags, and have the writer fix them.
4. For the other skills, publish the part as a page; the curator reads it whole. For the coordinator skill, land the change after its cold read, or put it on the page of skill drafts, as `SKILL.md`, "The curator's role and decisions", says.
5. Brief each comment of the curator to the writer, rather than rewrite it yourself. A comment marks a problem area: the writer fixes its paragraph or section, with the whole skill in mind.
6. Settle the writer's minor decisions from the record. On the other skills, ask the curator only where a rule would change its meaning or a new rule would enter. On the coordinator skill, `SKILL.md`, "The curator's role and decisions", says what waits.
7. After each change to the coordinator skill or to `fortress-repo` lands, have a worker update that skill's page: the page of skill drafts for the coordinator skill, the page of `fortress-repo` changes for `fortress-repo`. The boot note holds both links. Give the worker the page's URL, and have it publish by that URL. The record-landing workflow runs this update itself for the changes to `fortress-repo` that follow a landing (`references/batch.md`, "The landing", step 4). The page of skill drafts has two sections, and the page of `fortress-repo` changes has only the first:
   - Landed changes: one item for each change that landed since the curator's last approval on the page, or since the curator last said that they had read it, so that no change lands unseen while the curator is away. On the page of `fortress-repo` changes, which holds no approvals, the items start from the curator's last word that they have read it. The item takes the form of a landed item in `SKILL.md`, "Pages". For a change that waited for the curator's yes, it shows the change against the words that the curator approved. For any other change, it shows the change against the skill's text before it. It gives the change's reason, which may come from a cold read, a hit of the skills' lint, `explorations/coordinator/tools/skills-lint.py`, or the record entry that the orientation workflow, in update mode, took in. The reason says in plain words what was wrong and what the text now says. It never cites a cold read's flag by its code or number, a judge's ruling by its number, or an item of a task by its number.
   - Proposed changes: the items that wait for the curator's yes. An approved item leaves this section when it lands, and appears under the landed changes.

- Run `skill-writer.sh new <task-file>` for a fresh writer, and `skill-writer.sh resume <task-file>` for its next task, within the hour. Start a fresh writer after a pass over a whole skill, or after your compaction.
- The writer edits and commits the skill files. You push, except inside the record-landing workflow, which pushes the writer's commits itself. Keep each page in step: by a worker (step 7), the page of skill drafts for the coordinator skill and the page of `fortress-repo` changes for `fortress-repo`; and the part's page of step 4 for `cloud-container`.
- If a part that the curator approved is written again, have a Fable reviewer compare the two. Where it finds a regression, it writes a synthesis of both, never a wholesale revert.
- After a rule enters a skill from the curator's words, check that the skill caught the meaning, by a cold read or a test.
- If a practice that a skill states is in question, have a Sonnet scout check what the workers actually did. If they found a better way, write that way into the skill.
- Keep batch structure out of `fortress-repo`. The workflow or the brief sets which roles exist, and who builds, checks, commits and pushes.
- After each landing, the orientation workflow updates `fortress-repo`'s `references/revival-changes.md` (`references/batch.md`, "The landing", step 4). `fortress-repo`'s `SKILL.md` keeps only what does not change from batch to batch.

## The coordinator skill

This skill is rewritten by a heavier method, since the roles that it holds must not be lost:

- In the list of kept rules that goes into the writer's task (below), put how to talk to the curator in each situation, as a principle.
- Organize the record as the model organizes knowledge by itself, never against it. This is the rewrite's highest risk.
- Name the session's modes first: here, the six parts.
- Run the baseline interview (`explorations/coordinator/baseline-interview/README.md`) for each new model of this session. Keep only what the model would not do by itself.
- Keep a rule if the failure that it guards against is on record. The interview alone drops nothing.
- Write the list of kept rules into the writer's task. The writer writes from scratch, without reading the old skill. A worker then checks the draft against that list, and the cold read follows.

# Rewriting a skill

The skills are written for a reader new to the repository, which every agent is. A skill is a minimal set: it holds only the change to what the model does by itself, and leans on what its training already does well. Each rule states a goal or a principle, with the benefit that it brings, and the reader applies it with judgement. A rule is not a program of steps and conditions. A principle with its reason reaches the cases that it does not name. Many instructions, each for its own case, conflict, and the reader must then settle which one holds.

**writer**
: Headless session that makes every edit of the project skills, started and resumed by `explorations/coordinator/tools/skill-writer.sh`, with its standing brief `explorations/coordinator/skill-writer-brief.md`.

**cold read**
: Reading of a rewritten part by a worker given only the skill (`explorations/coordinator/skill-cold-read-brief.md`). It flags each passage that would send it wrong or make it search, with its confidence, and each undefined term.

## The method

1. Draft the outline first, with a home for every rule that moves.
2. Have the writer write each part whole, by the seven principles of `explorations/reviews/skills-writing-principles.md`. A rewrite is never longer than the text that it replaces.
3. Run a cold read. Review its flags, and have the writer fix them.
4. For the other skills, publish the part as a page; the curator reads it whole. For `fortress-repo`, this holds for a whole part that waits for the curator's yes; once it lands, its changes show on the page of `fortress-repo` changes (step 7). For the coordinator skill, land the change after its cold read, or put it on the page of skill drafts, as `SKILL.md`, "The curator's role and decisions", says.
5. Brief each comment of the curator to the writer, rather than rewrite it yourself. A comment marks a problem area: the writer fixes its paragraph or section, with the whole skill in mind.
6. Settle the writer's minor decisions from the record. On the other skills, ask the curator only where a rule would change its meaning or a new rule would enter. On the coordinator skill, `SKILL.md`, "The curator's role and decisions", says what waits.
7. After each change to the coordinator skill or to `fortress-repo` lands, have a worker update that skill's page: the page of skill drafts for the coordinator skill, the page of `fortress-repo` changes for `fortress-repo`. The boot note holds both links. Give the worker the page's URL, and have it publish by that URL. The record-landing workflow runs this update itself for the changes to `fortress-repo` that follow a landing (`references/batch.md`, "The landing", step 4). The page of skill drafts has two sections, and the page of `fortress-repo` changes has only the first:
   - Landed changes: one item for each change that landed since the curator's last approval on the page, or since the curator last said that they had read it, so that no change lands unseen while the curator is away. On the page of `fortress-repo` changes, which holds no approvals, the items start from the curator's last word that they have read it. The item takes the form of a landed item in `SKILL.md`, "Pages". For a change that waited for the curator's yes, it shows the change against the words that the curator approved. For any other change, it shows the change against the skill's text before it. It gives the change's reason, which may come from a cold read, a hit of the skills' lint, `explorations/coordinator/tools/skills-lint.py`, or the record entry that the orientation workflow, in update mode, took in. The reason says in plain words what was wrong and what the text now says. It never cites a cold read's flag by its code or number, a judge's ruling by its number, or an item of a task by its number.
   - Proposed changes: the items that wait for the curator's yes. An approved item leaves this section when it lands, and appears under the landed changes.

- Run `skill-writer.sh new <task-file>` for a fresh writer, and `skill-writer.sh resume <task-file>` for its next task, within the hour. Start a fresh writer after a pass over a whole skill, or after your compaction.
- The writer edits and commits the skill files. You push, except inside the record-landing workflow, which pushes the writer's commits itself. Keep each page in step: by a worker (step 7), the page of skill drafts for the coordinator skill and the page of `fortress-repo` changes for `fortress-repo`; and the part's page of step 4 for `cloud-container`.
- If a part that the curator approved is written again, have a Fable reviewer compare the two. Where it finds a regression, it writes a synthesis of both, never a wholesale revert.
- After a rule enters a skill from the curator's words, check that the skill caught the meaning, by a cold read or a test.
- If a practice that a skill states is in question, have a Sonnet scout check what the workers actually did. If they found a better way, write that way into the skill.
- Keep batch structure out of `fortress-repo`. The workflow or the brief sets which roles exist, and who builds, checks, commits and pushes.
- After each landing, the orientation workflow updates `fortress-repo`'s `references/revival-changes.md` (`references/batch.md`, "The landing", step 4). `fortress-repo`'s `SKILL.md` keeps only what does not change from batch to batch.

## The coordinator skill

This skill is rewritten by a heavier method, since the roles that it holds must not be lost:

- In the list of kept rules that goes into the writer's task (below), put how to talk to the curator in each situation, as a principle.
- Organize the record as the model organizes knowledge by itself, never against it. This is the rewrite's highest risk.
- Name the session's modes first: here, the six parts.
- Run the baseline interview (`explorations/coordinator/baseline-interview/README.md`) for each new model of this session. Keep only what the model would not do by itself.
- Keep a rule if the failure that it guards against is on record. The interview alone drops nothing.
- Write the list of kept rules into the writer's task. The writer writes from scratch, without reading the old skill. A worker then checks the draft against that list, and the cold read follows.
- Have every cold reader of this skill read it as the coordinating session, which uses it, not as a worker new to the repository.

# Committing and pushing

**scratch**
: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, probe programs, lists and private caches folders.

Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.

## What to commit

- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
- In a fresh clone, `.claude/worktrees/` and `.claude/agents/` show as untracked, because the lines of `.git/info/exclude` that hide them are not in the clone. Do not commit them.
- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, which is gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.

## How to commit

Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:

    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>

- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:

      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB

  If your brief gives another session line, use it.

## Pushing

Push after every commit, so that a lost container loses nothing.

- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
  3. If it lists only your commits, push three times, in this order:

         git push origin main
         git push origin main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8
         git push origin main:blinded-fable

     The third push keeps `blinded-fable` current. If the container is lost, the platform rebuilds it from that branch.
- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and say so in your report.

I made eight of the nine changes in two commits, which are not pushed. I skipped item 4 because the text already had it. The lint found no problems in the seven changed skill files.

**Commits:**
- `7aefb06ac`: the coordinator skill and the plan-consolidate README.
- `d7d81a2f1`: `fortress-repo`.

**Item 9 does not match the README.** The README's estimate said about 370,000 tokens, not 330,000. The boot note's "330K" is wrong.

**1. `batch.md`, "The landing", step 4.**
- Old: "…The workflow pushes the writer's commits, as its Land stage pushes the record's. Last, it has a worker update the page of `fortress-repo` changes (…step 7). No step of yours comes between. Until the workflow's README lists a step of this chain, run that step yourself after the workflow ends."
- New: "…Then it has a worker update the page of `fortress-repo` changes (…step 7), and pushes the writer's commits, as its Land stage pushes the record's. No step of yours comes between. Its result gives one line with the commits and the page's link (the README, "The skill update")."
- The old order had the push before the page. The new order is the README's: the page, then the push. The new text is shorter.

**2. `batch.md`, "The landing", the paragraph on a held push.**
- Old: "…take the steps below at once on the local commits. Only the push waits, and the parts of the routing that need the pushed hashes."
- New: "…take steps 1 to 3 at once on the local commits. Only the push waits, the parts of the routing that need the pushed hashes, and step 4: the record-landing workflow pushes `main` itself, so run it only after the batch is pushed."

**3. The coordinator skill's `sources.md`.** I moved the line on the wait cap out of "Changes landed on 2026-11-02, evening". It is now under a new heading, "The wait cap, 2026-11-03".
- `git log -S` shows that `3e3a5aef6` added the line on 2026-11-03 at 06:01 UTC.
- The heading "Changes landed on 2026-11-03" says that its lines come from the curator's messages. This line was settled by the coordinator, so I gave it a heading of its own.

**4. Skipped, already done.** `skill-rewrite.md` already points to "The landing", step 4, in two places. No pointer names step 5. An earlier line in `sources.md` records that fix on 2026-11-05.

**5. `skill-rewrite.md`, "The method".**
- Step 4 adds: "For `fortress-repo`, this holds for a whole part that waits for the curator's yes; once it lands, its changes show on the page of `fortress-repo` changes (step 7)."
- Step 7 adds: "For `cloud-container`, keep the part's page of step 4 in step in the same way." Step 7 is now the one place that says which page each skill keeps in step.
- The bullet after the steps loses its sentence "Keep each page in step: by a worker (step 7), the page of skill drafts…; and the part's page of step 4 for `cloud-container`."

**6. `SKILL.md`, "The boot".** I added a paragraph before "At a landing":
- "**The transcript backup.** At every boot and after every VM restart, read the last line of `.backup.log` and the date of the last snapshot (`git -C … log -1 --format=%ci`). Compare them with the machine's last start (`uptime -s`). If the snapshot is older than the last start, re-arm the backup before any other work (the `cloud-container` skill, `references/container-loss.md`, "Re-arming the backup"). The backup can fail with no message: it once stopped for about 18 hours, and a full boot did not notice."
- The paragraph gives the full path of `.backup.log`.
- It is a paragraph and not a numbered step for two reasons. A new number would change the step numbers that the light boot and `sources.md` use. The check also applies after a VM restart, which is not a boot.

**7. `delegating.md`, "What a brief holds".** I added a bullet: "The people of the project by their roles as the record gives them, never by a description of your own. A worker copies such a description: a brief once called a designer of Fortress's front end an outsider who knows a little of Fortress, and the worker put that designer's name to those words on a page."

**8. `fortress-repo`, `committing.md`, "Pushing", step 3.**
- Old: "push three times, in this order:" and three `git push` lines.
- New: "push the three refs in one command, in this order, in the foreground, and read its output. A loop that piped each push through `tail` once hid every failure." It is followed by `git push origin main main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8 main:blinded-fable`.
- "The third push keeps…" became "The third ref keeps…".

**9. The plan-consolidate README, "The estimate in tokens written".**
- The reader's row changed from "about 60,000" to "79,000, measured".
- The checker's row changed from "about 80,000" to "150,000, measured".
- The total changed from "about 370,000, between 300,000 and 450,000" to "509,000, measured in the run of 2026-11-03".

**Provenance:** The coordinator skill's `sources.md` has a new section, "Changes of 2026-11-05, evening", with one line for each of items 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 and 7. `fortress-repo`'s `sources.md` has a new section, "The push in one command, 2026-11-05", for item 8. The README has no provenance line, as the task said.

**Decisions not taken:**
- **Item 8, a refused push.** The bullet "If a push is refused, push nothing more" now applies to one command that pushes three refs. Git can update some refs of that command and refuse others. One option is to keep the bullet as it is. The other is to say: "If the command refuses a ref, push nothing more, and report which refs it updated."
- **Item 9, the paragraph under the table.** It still compares the old estimate with the inventory's estimate. One option is to keep it as history. The other is to cut it, now that the total is measured.
- **Item 9, the other rows.** Seven rows are still estimates. They add up to 230,000, so the reader and the checker were not the only steps over their estimates. A row for each step needs the run's logs.

**Things that differ from the task:**
- Item 4 was already done.
- Item 9's reason gave 330K for the README's old estimate, but the README said 370K.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# skills.sh N ROUND [--dry-run]: one round of the record-landing workflow's skill update, after the landing and
# the orientation update; its Sonnet driver runs it in the background and waits for it.
#
# Round 1 writes the skill writer's task, task-1.md, from skill-task.md and the landing's data, and starts a fresh
# skill writer on it (../skill-writer.sh new). The data, all from the main tree after the landing:
#   - the skill sentences that the landing made false: the landed diff.md's section "For the skill writer", if it
#     has one, and the bullets of its "For the coordinator" that name the skill; the same bullets of owed.md, the
#     sort's fuller list; and each "For the skill writer" section of the two writers' reports;
#   - diff.md's "POSITIONS", the changed words of the curator's decisions;
#   - the orientation update's folder: judgement.md, if its judge ran, and admission.md.
# If no line names the skill and the orientation's judge did not run, it starts no writer and prints NOTHING.
# Round 2 writes task-2.md from skill-fixes.md and the cold read's report, cold-read.md, and resumes the same
# writer (../skill-writer.sh resume). Each round saves the writer's report as writer-ROUND.md and its errors as
# writer-ROUND.log (ignored), then prints BASE (main's head before round 1, kept in base.txt), a COMMIT line for
# each commit since BASE that touches .claude/skills/, and a PART line for each skill file they changed, its
# sources.md left out, since a line of provenance needs no cold read.
# The folder is explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/skills/ in the main tree. The writer's session is kept
# under tmp/record-landing-N/skill-writer/ (SKILL_WRITER_STATE), so that the run leaves the coordinator's own
# writer session as it was. A round whose writer-ROUND.md holds a report is not run again. --dry-run prints the
# task and starts nothing.
set -uo pipefail
here=$(cd "$(dirname "$(readlink -f "$0")")" && pwd)
repo=$(cd "$here/../../../.." && pwd)
N=${1:?usage: skills.sh N ROUND [--dry-run]}; ROUND=${2:?round: 1 or 2}; DRY=${3:-}
CB="$repo/explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-$N"
SK="$CB/skills"; RL="$CB/record-landing"; OUT="$CB/orientation"
export SKILL_WRITER_STATE="$repo/tmp/record-landing-$N/skill-writer"
[ -f "$RL/diff.md" ] || { echo "skills.sh: no landed diff.md: $RL/diff.md" >&2; exit 1; }
case "$ROUND" in 1|2) ;; *) echo "skills.sh: the round is 1 or 2" >&2; exit 2 ;; esac

32	## The go
33	
34	- The batches of PLAN's phase 3 run on a standing go, in PLAN's order. Launch each when the batch before it has landed and its own batch record has no open question.
35	- If a question that the batch record raises is consequential (`SKILL.md`), put it to the curator first. Otherwise decide it and put it on the review list. While the curator is away, overnight, take its recommended default and put it on the review list. If that default would reverse a decision of the curator, hold that batch, and launch the repair batch (`explorations/coordinator/REPAIR-BATCH.md`) in its place.
36	- Have one Fable review read each coming batch record before the launch, with a go in advance. It is written for the curator in place of reading the record. Treat its questions as the batch record's.
37	
38	## The workflow
39	
40	- Between batches, improve the script and the manual where a batch showed a problem.
41	- Let every step spend the fewest workers that it needs.
42	- Build the base once, yourself, in a worktree where nobody compiles or runs (`args.baseBuild`). Every rung worktree is seeded from it (`explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh`), never built clean.
43	- No stage runs a build, a suite or a measurement again on a code state that another stage ran, and no agent reads again a log that has not changed.
44	- Let the planner give each rung its mission briefing, from the territory map (`explorations/coordinator/map/`), in neutral words: "the decisions on record", not the curator's name. Require no answers from the worker about how it searched.
45	- At each landing, report the share of briefed agents that read the briefing at all. Aim for all of them. By the brief's order, none reads it in its first turn.
46	
47	## The roles
48	
49	- The skeptic checks a rung's result after its worker, and builds nothing to check. It reads from the worker's transcript whether the test came first and failed. It runs its own small programs on the rung's build, and on the base through `explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh` with a private caches folder. Where the rung changes the compiled checker, the skeptic also runs the count stage itself, on the base build and on the worker's commits, as `fortress-repo`'s `compiler.md`, "The checker's time", gives a reviewer. That run is the one exception to this bullet and to the rule that no stage measures a code state again.
50	- It checks the result against the library's way, the ledger, sibling sites and the decisions on record, and fixes what it finds, test first.
51	- A judge rules only on a fix that the skeptic marks contested, on a rung that the skeptic refuses, or on a rung whose worker reported that it could not go on. The first ruling runs on Opus, a second on Fable (`judgeTier`). A settled fix lands with the review and the gate as its check. Reaching a reserved point, or a file outside what the rung's section of the batch record names, does not make a settled fix contested: it lands, and the point or the file goes on the review list. A point that cannot be undone holds the batch.
52	- No batch compares the printed outputs of the suites' test programs, and no baseline is run to compare against.
53	
54	## The checker count and the distance
55	
56	Until the switch-over lands, the gate of every batch reports the checker count and the distance. Neither turns the gate red.
57	
58	- If a rung's test is the checker count or the distance, it takes the last landed gate's tables as its starting values.
59	- If every file that a rung changes lies outside what the two measures read, the rung runs neither and lists those files (`STAGE_BLIND`). Its skeptic checks the list against the branch's diff.
60	- The review after the batch ties every new or risen row of the count's table to a named rung edit.
61	- The gate's comparisons hide Java line numbers, identity hashes and moved library positions. Put every difference that they hid on the review list. Put there too each line of the team's tests that a rung rewrote to keep its checked value, with its before and after.
62	
63	## Reserved points and repairs
64	
65	- A reversible reserved point does not hold the batch. The batch lands with the point's default, and the point goes on the review list.
66	- An output that the base already varies from run to run, with the test's verdict unchanged, is a ledger row.
67	- After its one repair round, a merged-diff review that still blocks does not hold a batch whose gate is green. Its findings go on the review list, for the batch after. The review runs once in each batch.
68	- A repair after the gate runs the gate again only if it changes what the gate reads (its part in `fortress-repo`).
69	- If the gate over a merged batch is red, do not bisect. Find the cause as a whole, and rework that part in the merged batch. If the gate is still red after its repair, the batch does not land: put it to the curator at once, as a hold.
70	
71	## While it runs
72	
73	- At a boot, read the batch record's sections for the curator, the run's journal (`references/delegating.md`) at the run ID in the check-in file (below), and the times of its agents' transcripts in the session's `subagents/workflows/<run>/`.
74	- From the launch until the run ends, by landing, by stopping or by holding its push for the curator, edit no tracked file in the main tree, the boot note included. The gather needs `git status --porcelain` there to print nothing. Keep `origin/main` at or behind the main tree's head, or git refuses the commit stage's push. So push `main` from no other tree. From the main tree, push nothing that the batch committed: the commit stage pushes it.
75	- Before the launch, name the check-in file in the boot note: `<scratchpad>/batch<N>/checkins.txt`, where `<N>` is the batch's number. After the launch, write the run's ID and each armed check-in's ID in that file. If the scratchpad loses a check-in's ID, find the check-in again with `list_triggers`.
76	- Workers push to their own `wip/` branches as they go. A branch holds only what `main` is to hold (`fortress-repo`, its committing part).
77	- If a process stop or the usage limit ends the run, resume it (`references/delegating.md`). The limit drops no rung.

explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md:201:There is one judge and one repair for the review, and no second review. When the review's repair returns nothing, stops or does not land, the code findings the judge upheld are listed as `review-unrepaired.N` for the next batch. They do not hold the push (the `coordinator` skill's `references/batch.md`, "Reserved points and repairs"). A step that cannot be undone that the repair reports holds it, as a rung's does.
explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md:252:## Commit, and the push held
explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md:263:The push is held when any landed rung's worker or skeptic, the review, or a merged-tree repair reports a point with `holdsPush` true, or a malformed one: a step that cannot be undone or acts against a decision on record. The stage then pushes nothing, keeps the worktrees, and writes a "Not pushed." paragraph into `RECORD.md`; the coordinator pushes once the curator lifts it. Batch 5's push went out past an unlifted stop because nothing held it (`compile-ladder/climb-batch-5/RECORD.md`). A rung that did not land holds nothing.
explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md:269:1. **The review's judge may land and route.** A ruling whose every upheld finding is settled by tests and records only is `land`: no repair runs, and its steps go to the next batch. In batch N the repair and second review for two such findings held the batch 54 minutes after a green gate and cost about 1.0M.
explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md:281:2. The routing: every open row, record default and item for the curator filed with a batch or as a parked line of `PLAN.md`. Each is checked against POSITIONS and the notes `INDEX.md` lists before it is called open, put to the curator or briefed. In the same pass the routing moves out of `PLAN.md` each item the batch built or answered, and any item it finds stale: word for word, into `PLAN-history.md`, under the landing's dated heading and the heading the item stood under. The batch's own line in its phase becomes one line, with its landing commit and its review. An open item whose text also stands in another home (a `review-queue.md` entry, a ledger row, a FACTS or POSITIONS entry) becomes one line in `PLAN.md`: what is asked, its default, and a pointer to that home. No other step takes an item out of `PLAN.md`, which held 519K characters before its consolidation of 2026-10-15, 54 % of them closed (`process-engineering/plan-map.md`, sections 2 and 4).
explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md:311:Once stopped, `callAgent` throws at the head of every attempt without starting an agent. No rung is marked dropped, withheld or not landed, and the gather does not start. The error says how to resume: `resumeFromRunId` with the same script and args, once the cause is gone. The finished agents come back from the journal.

# Rewriting a skill

The skills are written for a reader new to the repository, which every agent is. A skill is a minimal set: it holds only the change to what the model does by itself, and leans on what its training already does well. Each rule states a goal or a principle, with the benefit that it brings, and the reader applies it with judgement. A rule is not a program of steps and conditions. A principle with its reason reaches the cases that it does not name. Many instructions, each for its own case, conflict, and the reader must then settle which one holds.

**writer**
: Headless session that makes every edit of the project skills, started and resumed by `explorations/coordinator/tools/skill-writer.sh`, with its standing brief `explorations/coordinator/skill-writer-brief.md`.

**cold read**
: Reading of a rewritten part by a worker given only the skill (`explorations/coordinator/skill-cold-read-brief.md`). It flags each passage that would send it wrong or make it search, with its confidence, and each undefined term.

## The method

1. Draft the outline first, with a home for every rule that moves.
2. Have the writer write each part whole, by the seven principles of `explorations/reviews/skills-writing-principles.md`. A rewrite is never longer than the text that it replaces.
3. Run a cold read. Review its flags, and have the writer fix them.
4. For the other skills, publish the part as a page; the curator reads it whole. For `fortress-repo`, this holds for a whole part that waits for the curator's yes; once it lands, its changes show on the page of `fortress-repo` changes (step 7). For the coordinator skill, land the change after its cold read, or put it on the page of skill drafts, as `SKILL.md`, "The curator's role and decisions", says.
5. Brief each comment of the curator to the writer, rather than rewrite it yourself. A comment marks a problem area: the writer fixes its paragraph or section, with the whole skill in mind.
6. Settle the writer's minor decisions from the record. On the other skills, ask the curator only where a rule would change its meaning or a new rule would enter. On the coordinator skill, `SKILL.md`, "The curator's role and decisions", says what waits.
7. After each change to the coordinator skill or to `fortress-repo` lands, have a worker update that skill's page: the page of skill drafts for the coordinator skill, the page of `fortress-repo` changes for `fortress-repo`. The boot note holds both links. Give the worker the page's URL, and have it publish by that URL. For `cloud-container`, keep the part's page of step 4 in step in the same way. The record-landing workflow runs this update itself for the changes to `fortress-repo` that follow a landing (`references/batch.md`, "The landing", step 4). The page of skill drafts has two sections, and the page of `fortress-repo` changes has only the first:
   - Landed changes: one item for each change that landed since the curator's last approval on the page, or since the curator last said that they had read it, so that no change lands unseen while the curator is away. On the page of `fortress-repo` changes, which holds no approvals, the items start from the curator's last word that they have read it. The item takes the form of a landed item in `SKILL.md`, "Pages". For a change that waited for the curator's yes, it shows the change against the words that the curator approved. For any other change, it shows the change against the skill's text before it. It gives the change's reason, which may come from a cold read, a hit of the skills' lint, `explorations/coordinator/tools/skills-lint.py`, or the record entry that the orientation workflow, in update mode, took in. The reason says in plain words what was wrong and what the text now says. It never cites a cold read's flag by its code or number, a judge's ruling by its number, or an item of a task by its number.
   - Proposed changes: the items that wait for the curator's yes. An approved item leaves this section when it lands, and appears under the landed changes.

- Run `skill-writer.sh new <task-file>` for a fresh writer, and `skill-writer.sh resume <task-file>` for its next task, within the hour. Start a fresh writer after a pass over a whole skill, or after your compaction.
- The writer edits and commits the skill files. You push, except inside the record-landing workflow, which pushes the writer's commits itself.
- If a part that the curator approved is written again, have a Fable reviewer compare the two. Where it finds a regression, it writes a synthesis of both, never a wholesale revert.
- After a rule enters a skill from the curator's words, check that the skill caught the meaning, by a cold read or a test.
- If a practice that a skill states is in question, have a Sonnet scout check what the workers actually did. If they found a better way, write that way into the skill.
- Keep batch structure out of `fortress-repo`. The workflow or the brief sets which roles exist, and who builds, checks, commits and pushes.
- After each landing, the orientation workflow updates `fortress-repo`'s `references/revival-changes.md` (`references/batch.md`, "The landing", step 4). `fortress-repo`'s `SKILL.md` keeps only what does not change from batch to batch.

## The coordinator skill

This skill is rewritten by a heavier method, since the roles that it holds must not be lost:

- In the list of kept rules that goes into the writer's task (below), put how to talk to the curator in each situation, as a principle.
- Organize the record as the model organizes knowledge by itself, never against it. This is the rewrite's highest risk.
- Name the session's modes first: here, the six parts.
- Run the baseline interview (`explorations/coordinator/baseline-interview/README.md`) for each new model of this session. Keep only what the model would not do by itself.
- Keep a rule if the failure that it guards against is on record. The interview alone drops nothing.
- Write the list of kept rules into the writer's task. The writer writes from scratch, without reading the old skill. A worker then checks the draft against that list, and the cold read follows.
- Have every cold reader of this skill read it as the coordinating session, which uses it, not as a worker new to the repository.

# Committing and pushing

**scratch**
: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, probe programs, lists and private caches folders.

Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.

## What to commit

- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
- In a fresh clone, `.claude/worktrees/` and `.claude/agents/` show as untracked, because the lines of `.git/info/exclude` that hide them are not in the clone. Do not commit them.
- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, which is gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.

## How to commit

Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:

    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>

- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:

      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
